title: Complete problem for Search-SZK
formal:
Does Search-SZK, the class of promise search problems with statistical zero-knowledge protocols defined below, have a complete problem under the authors' deterministic polynomial-time Levin reductions? Precisely, is there one promise search problem \(R^{\star}\) such that
\[R^{\star}\in\mathrm{Search\text{-}SZK}\quad\text{and}\quad \forall R\in\mathrm{Search\text{-}SZK},\ R\le_{\mathrm L}^{\mathrm P}R^{\star}?\]
The user selected the statistical version on 16 September 2026. The source also asks the separate computational-zero-knowledge version; that question is not an additional required target here.
why: A complete problem would provide a single representative of statistical zero-knowledge search, as complete decision problems do for familiar complexity classes. The issue tests whether privacy of a revealed solution admits a common reduction-based structure even when protocols can produce many different legal outputs.

sentences: The question asks whether the authors’ statistical zero-knowledge search class has one complete promise search problem.
Protocols output a legal solution with perfect completeness and retain the source’s two soundness conditions.
A universal simulator receives one sample of the honest protocol’s output distribution and must reproduce any efficient verifier’s view up to negligible statistical distance.
Reductions must preserve yes and no promises and decode every legal target answer into a valid source answer.
Completeness is known for the Prefix-SZK subclass, while this card retains the full Search-SZK question selected by the user.

definitions:
A promise search problem is a pair \(R=(R_Y,L_N)\), where \(R_Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\times\{0,1\}^{*}\) is a binary relation and \(L_N\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\). Put
\[R_Y(x)=\{y:(x,y)\in R_Y\},\qquad L_Y=\{x:R_Y(x)\ne\varnothing\},\]
and require \(L_Y\cap L_N=\varnothing\). On a yes-instance \(x\in L_Y\), a valid answer is any \(y\in R_Y(x)\); on a no-instance \(x\in L_N\), it is the distinguished symbol \(\bot\), which is not a binary string. Inputs outside \(L_Y\cup L_N\) are outside the promise. No general polynomial-time test for membership in \(R_Y\) is assumed. Nor is this a total-search class: no-instances are permitted. The relation itself need not bound the length of every legal solution; a polynomial-time verifier can output only polynomially many bits on its own runs.

A protocol \((P,V)\) has a common binary input \(x\), classical messages and independent private fair random bits. The honest verifier \(V\) is one uniform probabilistic polynomial-time interactive Turing machine: its running time, communication and output length on every execution are bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(|x|\). A computationally unbounded prover \(P\) interacts with it; prover computation is not charged to verifier time. Malformed or overlong messages may cause rejection. The verifier outputs a binary string or \(\bot\). Write \((P,V)(x)\) for that output distribution, over the parties' random choices. There is no setup, shared secret, oracle or advice.

The authors' Search-IP conditions, retained exactly, are:
\[\forall x\in L_Y,\qquad \Pr[(P,V)(x)\in R_Y(x)]=1;\]
\[\forall P^{*}\ \forall x\in L_N,\qquad \Pr[(P^{*},V)(x)=\bot]\ge\tfrac12;\]
\[\forall P^{*}\ \forall x\in L_Y,\qquad \Pr[(P^{*},V)(x)\in R_Y(x)\cup\{\bot\}]\ge\tfrac12.\]
The first is perfect completeness. The other two quantify over all cheating prover strategies without a computational restriction. Thus a cheating prover must not force an invalid output with probability greater than one half, even on a yes-instance with some valid solutions. The source does not give a general soundness-amplification theorem for this search definition; the threshold is not silently replaced by negligible error.

For any uniform probabilistic polynomial-time cheating verifier \(V^{*}\), its view \(\operatorname{View}_{P,V^{*}}(x)\) is the explicitly encoded tuple of \(x\), its private random tape used in the execution, and all exchanged messages. The honest prover is used in this interaction. No external auxiliary input is supplied to \(V^{*}\).

Search-SZK requires a single universal simulator \(S\). Given \(x\), a finite description \(\langle V^{*}\rangle\) and one sample \(Y_x\) from the honest-output distribution \((P,V)(x)\), it produces a simulated view. For each fixed polynomial-time verifier \(V^{*}\), this simulation has expected running time polynomial in \(|x|\) on the stated inputs; the polynomial may depend on that verifier and the fixed protocol. This is the usual simulator convention when the verifier program, whose own polynomial time bound may vary, is supplied as a parameter. The simulator is one algorithm, not a separately chosen program for each verifier.

For every such \(V^{*}\) there must be a negligible function \(\eta_{V^{*}}\) such that, on every \(x\in L_Y\),
\[\Delta\bigl(\operatorname{View}_{P,V^{*}}(x),\ S(x,\langle V^{*}\rangle,Y_x)\bigr)\le\eta_{V^{*}}(|x|).\]
For distributions on encoded finite strings, \(\Delta(U,W)=\tfrac12\sum_z|\Pr[U=z]-\Pr[W=z]|\). A nonnegative function \(\eta\) is negligible if for every integer \(k\ge1\) there exists \(n_k\) such that \(\eta(n)\le n^{-k}\) for all \(n\ge n_k\). The bound is worst-case over yes-inputs of a given length, not an average over input distributions. All sampling coins are fresh; on the simulator side the honest sample and the simulator's coins are independent. The sample is from the protocol's own honest output law, not from an arbitrary distribution on legal solutions or from the cheating verifier's output. Statistical distance protects against all distinguishing tests, even computationally unbounded ones. The verifier being simulated nevertheless remains polynomial-time. No zero-knowledge requirement is imposed on no-instances or outside the promise.

For \(R=(R_Y,L_N)\) and \(Q=(Q_Y,K_N)\), the relation \(R\le_{\mathrm L}^{\mathrm P}Q\) means that there exist two uniform deterministic polynomial-time machines \(A,B\) satisfying
\[x\in L_Y\Longrightarrow A(x)\in K_Y,\qquad x\in L_N\Longrightarrow A(x)\in K_N,\]
\[\forall x\in L_Y\ \forall z\in Q_Y(A(x)),\qquad B(x,z)\in R_Y(x),\]
where \(K_Y=\{u:Q_Y(u)\ne\varnothing\}\). The time of \(A\) is polynomial in \(|x|\); that of \(B\) is polynomial in \(|x|+|z|\), using explicit binary encodings. Both halt on all inputs. There is one target instance and one answer transformation, with no randomness, advice or oracle. The decoder must work for every legal target answer, including answers that a particular target protocol never outputs. Outside the promise there is no correctness condition. The two programs and their polynomial bounds may depend on \(R\), but the complete problem \(R^{\star}\) is fixed before the universal quantifier over \(R\). The authors also define stronger solution-preserving reductions, requiring identical solution sets; that extra condition is not part of ordinary Levin completeness here.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed completeness claim. A positive answer must define one fixed promise search problem, establish a protocol and simulator satisfying the entire statistical definition, and prove that every Search-SZK problem has a Levin reduction to it with both promise directions and correctness for every valid target solution. A negative answer must show that no member of Search-SZK can be such a complete problem: for every candidate in the class, some Search-SZK problem fails to reduce to it. Completeness of decision-SZK, a restricted search subclass, or the computational search variant is not enough. Changing the simulator's sample distribution, adding auxiliary-input requirements or changing soundness requires an equivalence proof before it can answer this card. The target is unconditional and unrelativized; all probability and quantifier requirements are exact, without numerical tolerance.

context_blocks.text: A decision zero-knowledge protocol answers whether an instance has a property. A search protocol must return an actual solution while revealing no more than a sample of the solution that the honest protocol would produce. The intended disclosure therefore includes an output distribution, not only a yes/no answer.

Many legal answers may exist, and the prover’s soundness obligation is meaningful even when the input is a yes-instance: a cheating prover should not convince the verifier to output an invalid answer. The original one-half error bound is retained because repeated search executions can return different answers, and the paper does not infer the ordinary decision-protocol amplification rule.

The simulator is given one honest-protocol output sample. It is not guaranteed simulation from every individual valid answer, and it receives no external auxiliary information. The paper explicitly distinguishes these choices from other possible zero-knowledge definitions.

The paper defines a subclass called Prefix-SZK, where the prover first supplies a solution and then proves a suitable decision statement about it in statistical zero knowledge. Section 4.1 gives a complete problem for this subclass, even under the stronger solution-preserving reductions. It does not establish a complete problem for the entire Search-SZK class.

Ordinary Levin reductions preserve both sides of the promise and recover a valid source answer from every valid target answer. A complete problem would therefore provide one universal representative for the class’s search tasks, with precise control over solutions rather than just over accept/reject decisions.

The original draft combined statistical and computational completeness questions. The user selected the statistical question on 16 September 2026. The computational variant remains part of the source history, not a second success condition for this card.
